_source: Documented prescribing cascade pairs from peer-reviewed pharmacology literature. Sources: Rochon & Gurwitz (1997, 2017), Kalisch et al. (2011), Ontario Drug Policy Research Network, Canadian Deprescribing Network.
_note: symptomKeyword is a lowercase searchable fragment — multiple aliases per cascade pair are listed as separate entries to maximise keyword matching coverage.

cascades.description: Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine) cause peripheral oedema / ankle/leg swelling as a direct vasodilatory side effect. This is commonly mistaken for new-onset heart failure or venous insufficiency, triggering unnecessary diuretic prescriptions — a classic prescribing cascade.

Ankle oedema caused by dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine) is a direct drug side effect, not a sign of cardiac decompensation. Initiating a loop diuretic to treat it constitutes a well-documented prescribing cascade.

NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) can cause sodium and water retention, leading to ankle and leg oedema. This is often misidentified as heart failure, leading to inappropriate diuretic initiation.

Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs (zolpidem), and sedating antihistamines (diphenhydramine) frequently cause acute or subacute cognitive impairment in older adults. This is often misinterpreted as new-onset dementia or delirium requiring antipsychotic treatment — a dangerous prescribing cascade.

Drugs with high anticholinergic burden (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, promethazine) impair central acetylcholine signalling, causing memory problems, disorientation, and confusion. This is a leading contributor to avoidable dementia misdiagnosis in older patients.

High anticholinergic load from medications like bladder agents (oxybutynin) and sedating antidepressants (amitriptyline) is associated with reversible cognitive decline and short-term memory impairment. A cascade occurs when cognitive symptoms are treated with cholinesterase inhibitors rather than deprescribing the offending agent.

Benzodiazepines and related sedatives are associated with anterograde amnesia and daytime cognitive impairment, which may be confused with early dementia and trigger inappropriate dementia workup or drug initiation.

Opioid-induced constipation (OIC) is universal with opioid analgesia (codeine, tramadol, morphine, oxycodone) and is caused by mu-opioid receptor activation in the gut wall. Treating OIC with laxatives rather than opioid dose reduction represents a recognised prescribing cascade.

Calcium channel blockers (particularly verapamil and diltiazem) reduce intestinal smooth muscle contractility, causing constipation. This is frequently misattributed to diet or ageing rather than the medication.

Anticholinergic drugs (bladder agents, tricyclic antidepressants, antihistamines) reduce salivary gland secretion, causing xerostomia (dry mouth). Dry mouth is often treated with artificial saliva products or mouth rinses rather than deprescribing the offending agent.

Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, imipramine) and some SSRIs cause dry mouth as a direct anticholinergic side effect. This is commonly unrecognised as drug-induced and leads to unnecessary dental or salivary gland evaluation.

Anticholinergics (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, diphenhydramine) block bladder detrusor muscarinic receptors, causing incomplete bladder emptying and urinary retention. In men, this is routinely misdiagnosed as worsening BPH, prompting tamsulosin prescriptions.

ACE inhibitors and diuretics (thiazides, furosemide) used for hypertension or heart failure can increase urinary frequency. This symptom is often misattributed to overactive bladder, triggering anticholinergic bladder agents — a well-documented cascade with cumulative side effect burden.

Loop and thiazide diuretics (furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide) cause increased urinary frequency as their primary mechanism of action. This is sometimes misinterpreted as overactive bladder and treated with anticholinergic agents, adding unnecessary drug burden.

Excessive blood pressure lowering or autonomic blunting causes orthostatic cerebral hypoperfusion when standing. Dizziness is misdiagnosed as inner-ear vertigo, prompting cinnarizine or betahistine prescriptions.

Sedatives and anxiolytics (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs) cause dose-dependent dizziness and gait instability. This is often misattributed to inner ear problems rather than the medication, leading to inappropriate antivertigo drug prescriptions.

Benzodiazepines and sedating antihistamines significantly increase fall risk in older adults through sedation, muscle relaxation, and impaired proprioception. Falls may trigger pain prescriptions (NSAIDs, opioids) as a cascade without addressing the root sedative cause.

Opioid analgesics (codeine, tramadol, morphine) stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone, causing nausea and vomiting in 25-40% of patients. This is a direct drug side effect that is commonly treated with antiemetic prescriptions (metoclopramide, ondansetron) — a prescribing cascade.

Direct chemical irritation and systemic COX-1 inhibition reduce gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion, causing severe heartburn and dyspepsia. Frequently managed by adding chronic PPI therapy rather than deprescribing the NSAID.

NSAID-related gastrointestinal symptoms (stomach pain, dyspepsia, reflux) are among the most common drug adverse effects. Prescribing a PPI or H2 blocker to manage NSAID-induced GI symptoms is the most frequently cited prescribing cascade pair in the literature.

Statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS) caused by mitochondrial coenzyme Q10 depletion manifest as diffuse bilateral myalgia. Patients frequently self-medicate or are prescribed NSAIDs, increasing gastrointestinal and renal toxicity.

Statin-induced myopathy can manifest as symmetrical proximal limb weakness. Clinicians may mistakenly attribute this to ageing or musculoskeletal conditions and prescribe analgesics or physiotherapy without addressing statin toxicity.
Unexplained generalized muscle aching from statins commonly triggers new orders for muscle relaxants or NSAIDs rather than statin dose reduction or holiday.

Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the striatum by first- and second-generation antipsychotics causes extrapyramidal symptoms including resting tremors. Frequently misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease, leading to inappropriate antiparkinsonian therapy (levodopa, trihexyphenidyl).
Lead-pipe or cogwheel muscle rigidity resulting from central dopamine antagonism is mistaken for idiopathic Parkinson's disease, creating an avoidable prescribing cascade.

Systemic corticosteroids stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis and induce peripheral insulin resistance, driving acute glucose elevations. Treating steroid-induced hyperglycemia with permanent antidiabetic regimens represents an avoidable cascade.
Steroid-induced hyperglycemia is often mistaken for new-onset Type 2 diabetes, leading to multiple glucose-lowering drugs (metformin, sulfonylureas, insulin).
Central beta-blockade and reduced cardiac output cause chronic lethargy and exercise intolerance. Misdiagnosed as clinical depression, prompting inappropriate antidepressant initiation.

Beta-blocker sympathetic inhibition and peripheral vasoconstriction frequently causes erectile dysfunction. Treating this with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) rather than switching to an ARB risks severe hypotensive interaction.

Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) and loop diuretics (furosemide) compete with uric acid at the renal organic acid transporter, elevating serum uric acid and precipitating acute gout attacks. Lifelong allopurinol is often started without reconsidering the diuretic.
Acute podagra from diuretic-induced hyperuricemia is frequently managed with anti-gout therapy without reviewing the causative diuretic dose.

SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) promote massive renal glucose excretion (glucosuria), creating a fertile environment for mycotic genital infections. Treating recurrent candidiasis with repetitive antifungals without patient glycemic counseling constitutes an SGLT2 cascade.
Glycosuria from SGLT2 inhibitors elevates the incidence of ascending bacterial UTIs. Repetitive antibiotic courses without reassessing diabetes therapy is an emerging cascade.

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) increase acetylcholine levels at bladder muscarinic receptors, provoking urinary urge incontinence. Prescribing anticholinergic bladder agents (oxybutynin, tolterodine) directly neutralizes the cognitive benefit and accelerates dementia.
Detrusor hyperactivity from excess cholinergic tone causes sudden urinary leakage, often treated with antimuscarinics that cause severe cognitive decline in dementia patients.

Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine) cause precapillary arteriolar vasodilation and hydrostatic fluid extravasation, presenting as pedal edema. Misdiagnosed as congestive heart failure, prompting inappropriate diuretic prescription.
Swelling of feet and lower extremities is a classic adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Treating this with loop diuretics represents a classic prescribing cascade.
Peripheral fluid accumulation from calcium channel blockers is frequently mistaken for renal or cardiac decompensation, leading to unnecessary diuretic prescribing.
NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac) inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, impairing sodium excretion and inducing dependent peripheral edema often treated inappropriately with loop diuretics.

NSAIDs blunt renal vasodilation, promoting sodium and water retention and attenuating the effects of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers. Blood pressure spikes are often treated by adding another antihypertensive agent rather than stopping the NSAID.
Systemic vasoconstriction and volume expansion from chronic NSAID use causes sustained elevation of arterial blood pressure, precipitating antihypertensive dose escalation.
NSAIDs weaken mucosal defenses in the stomach and lower esophagus, exacerbating acid reflux symptoms and triggering proton pump inhibitor initiation.
Gastric mucosal damage caused by NSAIDs produces persistent epigastric burning pain, leading to chronic acid-suppression therapy.
Indigestion and epigastric discomfort from NSAID therapy are frequently treated with H2 blockers or PPIs rather than considering safer topical or paracetamol alternatives.

ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril) prevent the degradation of bradykinin and substance P in bronchial tissues, inducing a persistent dry, hacking cough in up to 20% of patients. Often misdiagnosed as asthma, allergy, or bronchitis and treated with ineffective antitussives or inhalers instead of switching to an ARB.

A chronic, non-productive dry cough is a hallmark adverse effect of ACE inhibitors. Inappropriate prescribing cascades include prescribing codeine, dextromethorphan, or antihistamines instead of substituting with losartan or telmisartan.
Persistent tickling sensation in the throat caused by bradykinin accumulation from ACE inhibitors is frequently treated with lozenges, allergy pills, or antibiotics.
Hyperuricemic crystalline arthritis from diuretic use manifests as acute joint inflammation, commonly triggering NSAID or colchicine prescriptions.
Classic podagra (acute gout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint) triggered by diuretic volume contraction and uric acid reabsorption, leading to unnecessary chronic urate-lowering therapy.
Asymptomatic or symptomatic elevation of serum uric acid induced by diuretic therapy, frequently treated with allopurinol or febuxostat instead of diuretic dose reduction.

Renal potassium and magnesium wasting from loop diuretics (furosemide) causes nocturnal leg and calf muscle cramps. Patients are prescribed large oral potassium chloride tablets that carry severe gastrointestinal ulceration risks.
Electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) from high-dose diuretics leads to painful leg spasms, often treated with quinine, muscle relaxants, or mineral pills.
Drug-induced extrapyramidal tremors from antipsychotics or antiemetics (metoclopramide) lead to unnecessary neurological consultations and dopaminergic prescriptions.
Akathisia (an intense internal urge to move) caused by neuroleptics is often misinterpreted as worsening psychiatric anxiety or psychosis, prompting dosage increases or adding sedatives.
Increased bladder contractility induced by dementia drugs is misattributed to overactive bladder or aging, initiating a dangerous anticholinergic prescribing cascade.
Opioids inhibit sacral parasympathetic outflow and contract the urinary sphincter. Acute urinary retention is misidentified as an anatomical obstruction rather than opioid-induced.
Impaired bladder contractility from anticholinergic medications creates hesitancy and weak stream, triggering urological workups and alpha-blocker initiation.

Evening or high-dose corticosteroids disrupt the circadian cortisol rhythm, causing marked nocturnal insomnia and agitation that is treated with benzodiazepines or Z-drugs instead of shifting steroid doses to the morning.
Glucocorticoid-induced central nervous system stimulation causes severe sleep deprivation, prompting hypnotic prescriptions.

Beta-blockers antagonize bronchial beta-2 receptors, increasing airway resistance and provoking wheezing in vulnerable patients. Patients are prescribed bronchodilators instead of discontinuing the offending beta-blocker.
Drug-induced bronchoconstriction or blunted chronotropic response from beta-blockers causes dyspnea that is mistaken for asthma or heart failure, triggering additional inhalers or diuretics.
Persistent profound exhaustion from lipophilic beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol) is treated with energizing supplements or antidepressants rather than dose titration.
Statin myopathy is often misattributed to aging, sprains, or arthritis, leading to long-term analgesic use instead of statin dose reduction or CoQ10 co-supplementation.
Unexplained bilateral leg and shoulder soreness caused by statin therapy triggers inappropriate muscle relaxant or NSAID prescriptions.
Postural blood pressure drops from antihypertensives cause lightheadedness, leading to unnecessary neurological evaluations or midodrine initiation instead of deprescribing.
Orthostatic hypotension from polypharmacy antihypertensive regimens is a major cause of falls and hip fractures in elderly patients, leading to mobility aids and hospital admissions.

Chronic hypochlorhydria from long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy impairs active TRPM6/7 magnesium absorption, producing severe hypomagnesemic cramps, tetany, and cardiac arrhythmias treated with mineral supplements while the PPI is continued indefinitely.
Profound refractory hypomagnesemia caused by prolonged PPI therapy is treated with oral or intravenous magnesium replacements rather than tapering the acid suppressant.

Long-term metformin therapy impairs calcium-dependent ileal absorption of the Vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex, causing peripheral neuropathy. This is misdiagnosed as advancing diabetic polyneuropathy, triggering gabapentin or pregabalin prescriptions instead of B12 testing and repletion.
Metformin-induced Vitamin B12 deficiency neuropathy presents with symmetric paresthesias in the hands and feet, leading to inappropriate neuropathic pain medications.
Peripheral neuropathy symptoms from metformin-induced B12 malabsorption are treated symptomatically with gabapentin rather than addressing the nutritional deficiency.
Antagonism of 5-HT2C and H1 receptors by second-generation antipsychotics drives intense hyperphagia and rapid visceral weight gain, leading to the initiation of metformin or weight-loss drugs.
Severe drug-induced appetite stimulation causes rapid metabolic deterioration, predisposing to dyslipidemia and diabetes that are treated with multi-drug regimens.

Glucosuria induced by SGLT2 inhibitors promotes fungal candida proliferation in the perineal region, causing recurrent vulvovaginitis and balanitis treated with repeated courses of fluconazole or clotrimazole.
Genital mycotic infections from high urinary sugar excretion are treated with long-term antifungal therapy rather than enhanced hygiene or dosage adjustment.
SSRIs frequently cause acute serotonin-mediated gastric distress and SIADH-induced hyponatremia, leading to antiemetic prescriptions (ondansetron, domperidone).
SSRIs and SNRIs frequently cause postural hand tremors, which are mistakenly treated with beta-blockers like propranolol.
Chronic opioid therapy suppresses respiratory drive and central arousal mechanisms, causing severe daytime hypersomnolence and central sleep apnea, sometimes treated with stimulants.
Blockade of lacrimal gland muscarinic receptors causes severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes), triggering chronic artificial tear prescriptions.
